title: Data Wrangling with Tidyverse
text: This page demonstrates data wrangling techniques using the Tidyverse in R. The exercises cover filtering, reshaping, pivoting, handling missing values, and combining data wrangling with visualization — applied to real datasets including airquality, nycflights13, relig_income, and us_rent_income.

title: Data Wrangling with Tidyverse
section: Air Quality Data: Filtering and Selection
text:
Air Quality Data: Filtering and Selection
Working with R’s built-in airquality dataset to demonstrate both Tidyverse and base R approaches to data extraction.


Show code
air.tib <- as_tibble(airquality)

# Tidyverse approach: filter and select
air.tib %>%
  filter(Temp == 97) %>%
  select(Ozone)


# A tibble: 1 × 1
  Ozone
  <int>
1    76

title: Data Wrangling with Tidyverse
text:
NYC Flights: Worst Arrival Delays
Identifying the 10 worst daily arrival delays across all of 2013, then averaging them by month to reveal seasonal patterns.


Show code
library(nycflights13)

worst_delays <- flights %>%
  drop_na(arr_delay) %>%
  group_by(year, month, day) %>%
  slice_max(arr_delay, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avg_worst_delay = mean(arr_delay))

ggplot(worst_delays, aes(x = factor(month), y = avg_worst_delay)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3498db", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title = "Average of the 10 Worst Daily Arrival Delays by Month",
    subtitle = "NYC flights, 2013 — extreme delays are surprisingly consistent across months",
    x = "Month", y = "Average Delay (minutes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))









Insight: The average of the most extreme arrival delays remains relatively stable across months, with no dramatic seasonal pattern, suggesting that factors causing very large delays are not strongly tied to the time of year.

title: Data Wrangling with Tidyverse
text:
Reshaping Data: Religion and Income
Transforming the relig_income dataset from wide to long format for visualization, then creating a grouped bar chart showing income distributions across religious affiliations.


Show code
relig_long <- relig_income %>%
  pivot_longer(-religion, names_to = "income", values_to = "count") %>%
  filter(income != "Don't know/refused")

ggplot(relig_long, aes(x = religion, y = count, fill = income)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(preserve = "single")) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(
    title = "Income Distribution by Religious Affiliation",
    subtitle = "Data reshaped from wide to long format using pivot_longer()",
    x = "Religion", y = "Number of Respondents", fill = "Income Bracket"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

title: Data Wrangling with Tidyverse
text:
Rent vs. Income: Pivot Wider
Using pivot_wider() to reshape the us_rent_income dataset and explore the relationship between median income and median rent across US states.


Show code
us_rent_income %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = c(estimate, moe)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate_income, y = estimate_rent)) +
  geom_point(color = "#27ae60", size = 2.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Income vs. Median Rent Across US States",
    subtitle = "Strong positive relationship — higher income states have higher rents",
    x = "Median Income ($)", y = "Median Rent ($)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

title: Data Wrangling with Tidyverse
text:
Handling Missing Values
Demonstrating multiple strategies for identifying and replacing missing values in the airquality dataset using mean imputation.


Show code
air.tib <- as_tibble(airquality)

# Missing value summary
missing_summary <- air.tib %>%
  summarise(
    missing_n = sum(is.na(Solar.R)),
    missing_pct = round(mean(is.na(Solar.R)) * 100, 1)
  )

missing_summary %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_label(missing_n = "Missing Count", missing_pct = "Missing %") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Solar Radiation: Missing Value Summary")








Solar Radiation: Missing Value Summary


Missing Count
Missing %




7
4.6









Show code
# Compute rounded mean for imputation
solar_mean_rounded <- air.tib %>%
  summarise(avg = round(mean(Solar.R, na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
  pull(avg)

# Replace NAs with mean
air.tib <- air.tib %>%
  mutate(Solar.R = if_else(is.na(Solar.R), solar_mean_rounded, Solar.R))

# Verify
paste("Remaining NAs in Solar.R:", sum(is.na(air.tib$Solar.R)))

title: Data Wrangling with Tidyverse
text:
Temperature Analysis by Month
Aggregating temperature data by month and visualizing it with ordered bar charts.

Total TemperatureMaximum Temperature




Show code
air.tib %>%
  mutate(Month_name = case_when(
    Month == 5 ~ "May", Month == 6 ~ "June", Month == 7 ~ "July",
    Month == 8 ~ "August", Month == 9 ~ "September"
  )) %>%
  group_by(Month_name) %>%
  summarise(total_temp = sum(Temp, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = total_temp, y = fct_reorder(Month_name, total_temp))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#e74c3c", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(title = "Total Recorded Temperature by Month", x = "Total Temperature", y = "") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))













Show code
air.tib %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  summarise(max_temp = max(Temp, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(Month = recode(Month, `5` = "May", `6` = "June", `7` = "July",
                               `8` = "August", `9` = "September")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = max_temp, y = fct_reorder(Month, max_temp))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#f39c12", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(title = "Highest Temperature by Month", x = "Maximum Temperature (°F)", y = "") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

title: Data Wrangling with Tidyverse
text:
Multivariate Exploration: Ozone Relationships
Exploring how temperature, wind speed, and their ratio relate to ozone levels using faceted scatter plots.


Show code
air.tib %>%
  mutate(temp_wind = Temp / Wind) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Temp, Wind, temp_wind),
               names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "#3498db", size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Ozone vs. Temperature, Wind, and Their Ratio",
    subtitle = "Temperature drives ozone up; wind drives it down",
    x = "Variable Value", y = "Ozone (ppb)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









Conclusion: Ozone is positively associated with temperature and negatively associated with wind speed. The ratio Temp/Wind does not reveal a strong linear relationship, indicating that the individual effects of temperature and wind are more informative than their simple quotient.

title: Advanced Data Visualization
text: This page documents reflections on advanced data visualization principles and demonstrates key techniques learned through workshops by Thomas Lin Pedersen, David Robinson, and Cédric Scherer, as well as the gt and gtExtras table packages.

title: Advanced Data Visualization
text:
The Grammar of Graphics
The workshop by Thomas Lin Pedersen was transformative. The core insight was to treat plots not as monolithic final products, but as composable objects built from reusable parts. This philosophy, rooted in the grammar of graphics, demystifies complexity.

By consciously separating data, aesthetics, geoms, and guides, even the most intricate visualizations become manageable.

title: Advanced Data Visualization
text:
Scales and Transformations
Scales are the critical translators between your data and your audience. A plot’s ability to communicate honestly and effectively hinges on scale choices.


Show code
df <- data.frame(
  category = c("A", "B", "C"),
  value = c(10, 20, 1000)
)

p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = category, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3498db", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(title = "Linear Scale", subtitle = "Outlier dominates the view") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

p2 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = category, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#e74c3c", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Log10 Scale", subtitle = "Relative differences revealed") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

p1 + p2









The same data tells a completely different story depending on the scale. Linear scales can hide small but meaningful differences when outliers are present, while log scales reveal relative proportions.

title: Advanced Data Visualization
text:
Three Essential Functions
From David Robinson’s impromptu data visualization workflow, three functions stood out as essential for rapid exploratory analysis:

dplyr::count() — Quick Frequency Analysis


Show code
mpg %>%
  count(class) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(class, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2ecc71", alpha = 0.85) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Vehicle Class Distribution",
    subtitle = "count() provides instant frequency summaries",
    x = "Car Class", y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))











tidyr::separate() — Splitting Combined Fields


Show code
messy_df <- data.frame(id = 1:3, info = c("Model_A_Red", "Model_B_Blue", "Model_C_Green"))

clean_df <- messy_df %>%
  separate(info, into = c("prefix", "model", "color"), sep = "_")

clean_df %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(title = "Cleaned Data with separate()")

title: Advanced Data Visualization
text:
Tables as Data Products
The gt package redefined my perception of tables. A table can be more than a crude printout — it can be a sophisticated data product with its own visual appeal.

  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    avg_mpg = round(mean(mpg), 1),
    avg_hp = round(mean(hp), 0),
    avg_wt = round(mean(wt), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Engine Performance Summary",
    subtitle = "Grouped by number of cylinders"
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    cyl = "Cylinders",
    n = "Count",
    avg_mpg = "Avg MPG",
    avg_hp = "Avg HP",

title: Advanced Data Visualization
text:
Design Principles from Cédric Scherer
Three key principles for intentional, effective data visualization:

Use perceptually uniform palettes — Palettes like Viridis ensure that changes in color value are perceived as equal changes in data value, without introducing false visual emphasis.
Refine typography and space — Consistent font sizes, adjusted margins, and lighter gridlines create a clear visual hierarchy that guides the viewer’s eye without distraction.
Practice intentional annotation — Annotate sparingly. Highlight the two or three key data points, and let the rest of the data speak for itself.

title: Advanced Data Visualization
section: Life Expectancy: Top and Bottom 5 in Asia
text:
Life Expectancy: Top and Bottom 5 in Asia
Using patchwork to compose multiple plots into a single, coherent narrative.


Show code
library(gapminder)

asia_2007 <- gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007, continent == "Asia")

top5 <- asia_2007 %>% slice_max(lifeExp, n = 5)
bottom5 <- asia_2007 %>% slice_min(lifeExp, n = 5)

p1 <- ggplot(top5, aes(x = reorder(country, lifeExp), y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2ecc71", alpha = 0.85) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 5 Life Expectancy", x = "", y = "Life Expectancy (years)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

p2 <- ggplot(bottom5, aes(x = reorder(country, lifeExp), y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#e74c3c", alpha = 0.85) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Bottom 5 Life Expectancy", x = "", y = "Life Expectancy (years)") +

title: Data Visualization in R
section: Scatter Plot: Prior GPA vs. Missed Classes
text:
Scatter Plot: Prior GPA vs. Missed Classes
A faceted scatter plot examining whether the relationship between prior GPA and missed classes differs between sophomores and non-sophomores. The linear regression lines reveal a negative trend — higher GPA is associated with fewer missed classes — and the pattern holds across both groups.


Show code
df_sophomore_recoded <- df %>%
  mutate(soph = factor(ifelse(soph == "1", "Sophomore", "Non-Sophomore")))

df_sophomore_recoded %>%
  ggplot(aes(priGPA, missed)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "#2c3e50", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ soph) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Prior GPA and Missed Classes",
    subtitle = "Faceted by sophomore status — higher GPA correlates with fewer absences",
    x = "Prior GPA",
    y = "Number of Missed Classes"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)
  )

title: Data Visualization in R
text:
Comparing Bar Chart Types
A critical comparison of dodge, stacked, and faceted bar charts to determine which chart type most accurately represents the relationship between ACT scores, final exam performance, and sophomore status.

Dodge Chart (Means)Stacked Chart (Means)Faceted Chart (Means)




Show code
df_averages <- df %>%
  mutate(soph_label = factor(soph, levels = c(0, 1),
                             labels = c("Not Sophomore", "Sophomore"))) %>%
  group_by(ACT, soph_label) %>%
  summarise(mean_final = mean(final, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(df_averages, aes(x = ACT, y = mean_final, fill = soph_label)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Not Sophomore" = "#3498db", "Sophomore" = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean Final Score by ACT and Sophomore Status",
    subtitle = "Dodge chart using averaged scores — the most accurate representation",
    x = "ACT Score", y = "Mean Final Score", fill = "Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))













Show code
ggplot(df_averages, aes(x = ACT, y = mean_final, fill = soph_label)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Not Sophomore" = "#3498db", "Sophomore" = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean Final Score by ACT and Sophomore Status",
    subtitle = "Stacked chart — harder to compare individual group values",
    x = "ACT Score", y = "Mean Final Score", fill = "Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))













Show code
ggplot(df_averages, aes(x = ACT, y = mean_final, fill = soph_label)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(soph_label ~ .) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Not Sophomore" = "#3498db", "Sophomore" = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean Final Score by ACT and Sophomore Status",
    subtitle = "Faceted view — clear separation for individual group analysis",
    x = "ACT Score", y = "Mean Final Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#ecf0f1"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )












Key Finding: The dodge and faceted charts using averaged data accurately represent the underlying patterns. The stacked chart makes group comparison difficult. Higher ACT scores consistently predict higher final scores, and sophomores maintain a modest advantage across nearly all ACT levels.

title: Data Visualization in R
text:
Boxplot with Jittered Points
A boxplot enhanced with jittered individual data points provides the most comprehensive view — showing the median, spread, outliers, and the full distribution simultaneously.


Show code
ggplot(df_sophomore_recoded, aes(x = factor(ACT), y = final, fill = soph)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.7, width = 0.6) +
  geom_jitter(
    position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.2, dodge.width = 0.7),
    aes(color = soph), alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Non-Sophomore" = "#3498db", "Sophomore" = "#2ecc71")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Non-Sophomore" = "#2c3e50", "Sophomore" = "#27ae60")) +
  labs(
    title = "Final Scores by ACT and Sophomore Status",
    subtitle = "Boxplots reveal distribution spread; jittered points show individual observations",
    x = "ACT Score", y = "Final Score", fill = "Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )









Insight: Sophomores consistently outperform non-sophomores with slightly elevated medians across most ACT levels, suggesting additional academic experience contributes to stronger performance.

title: Data Visualization in R
text:
Attendance Rate by ACT Score
Examining how freshman status moderates the relationship between ACT scores and class attendance.


Show code
df_freshman_recoded <- df %>%
  mutate(
    freshman_label = factor(frosh, levels = c(0, 1),
                            labels = c("Non-Freshman", "Freshman"))
  )

ggplot(df_freshman_recoded, aes(x = ACT, y = atndrte)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "#3498db") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ freshman_label) +
  labs(
    title = "Attendance Rate vs. ACT Score",
    subtitle = "Freshmen attend less and show a weaker ACT–attendance relationship",
    x = "ACT Score", y = "Attendance Rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)
  )









Finding: Freshmen not only attend less across all ACT levels but also show a diminished response to ACT — the slope for freshmen is notably shallower, indicating that factors beyond academic aptitude drive their attendance patterns.

title: Data Visualization in R
text:
Correlation Analysis
A comprehensive correlation analysis of key academic variables using both a pairs matrix and a heatmap.


Show code
df_var <- df %>%
  select(attend, termGPA, priGPA, ACT, final, atndrte, hwrte)

ggcorr(df_var, label = TRUE, label_round = 2, hjust = 0.6, size = 4,
       layout.exp = 2) +
  labs(title = "Correlation Heatmap of Academic Variables") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14))









Key Findings:

Strongest correlation: attend and atndrte (r = 1.0) — these are directly derived from each other
Next strongest: termGPA and priGPA (r ≈ 0.7) — strong academic consistency
Attendance vs. homework for GPA: Attendance rate shows stronger correlations with both term and prior GPA than homework submission, suggesting that class attendance may be a more effective strategy for improving grades

title: Data Visualization in R
text:
Interactive Visualization
Using plotly to create an interactive scatter plot that allows exploration of the relationship between prior GPA and term GPA.


Show code
df_soph_labeled <- df %>%
  mutate(soph_label = factor(soph, levels = c(0, 1),
                              labels = c("Not Sophomore", "Sophomore")))

scatter_plt <- ggplot(df_soph_labeled, aes(x = priGPA, y = termGPA, color = soph_label)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Not Sophomore" = "#e74c3c", "Sophomore" = "#2c3e50")) +
  labs(
    title = "Prior GPA vs. Term GPA",
    subtitle = "Interactive — hover to explore individual data points",
    x = "Prior GPA", y = "Term GPA", color = "Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

ggplotly(scatter_plt, tooltip = c("x", "y", "color"))






A strong positive relationship exists between prior and current GPA across both class levels, demonstrating academic consistency regardless of sophomore status.

title: R Programming & Functional Programming
section: Nested Data & Map: Ozone by Month
text:
Nested Data & Map: Ozone by Month
Using nested data frames and map_dbl() to calculate average ozone by month — a functional programming pattern that avoids repetitive code.


Show code
calc_mean <- function(data) {
  mean(data$Ozone, na.rm = TRUE)
}

ozone_by_month <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    group_by(Month) %>%
    nest() %>%
    mutate(mean_ozone = map_dbl(data, calc_mean)) %>%
    select(Month, mean_ozone) %>%
    arrange(Month)
}

result <- ozone_by_month(airquality)

result %>%
  mutate(Month = recode(Month,
    `5` = "May", `6` = "June", `7` = "July",
    `8` = "August", `9` = "September"
  )) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Average Ozone by Month",
    subtitle = "Computed using nested data frames and map_dbl()"
  ) %>%
  cols_label(Month = "Month", mean_ozone = "Mean Ozone (ppb)") %>%
  fmt_number(columns = mean_ozone, decimals = 1)

    `5` = "May", `6` = "June", `7` = "July",
    `8` = "August", `9` = "September"
  )) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(Month_name, mean_ozone), y = mean_ozone)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#e67e22", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_ozone, 1)), hjust = -0.2, fontface = "bold") +

  ) +

  expand_limits(y = max(result$mean_ozone) * 1.15)









Key takeaway: Functional programming in R — using nested data, custom functions, and map() — eliminates repetitive code and makes analyses reproducible and scalable.
